newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe stresses Europe, gradual reform in programme.
newsitem.headline: Juppe stresses Europe, gradual reform in programme.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe outlined his centre-right coalition's programme for an early parliamentary election on Tuesday, stressing his commitment to Europe and to gradual, market-oriented economic reforms.

He gave a rousing defence of the planned single European currency, ruling out any delay in its launch set for 1999 and accusing the opposition Socialists of reneging on their European beliefs out of electoral opportunism.

"France has nothing to fear but everything to gain from the euro, everything to gain from the Union, everything to gain from Europe," Juppe said. "(We need) the euro now, because tomorrow will be too late."

Juppe sought to unite the often fractious coalition, praising the achievements of his conservative predecessor Edouard Balladur, who ran unsuccessfully against fellow Gaullist Jacques Chirac in a 1995 presidential election, splitting the Right.

The prime minister said he planned to run the campaign for the May 25-June 1 election on his vision of France's future rather than on his record, which has featured a relentless rise in unemployment to a record 12.8 percent.

"Employment has been, is and will remain our obsession," he said, boasting a fall in youth unemployment but acknowledging: "That obviously is not sufficient. Unemployment is not really going down because we are not yet creating enough jobs to meet the increase in the working population..."
Juppe said his coalition stood for France's modernisation while the left-wing opposition were the real conservatives since they wanted to return to archaic, failed, state-driven recipes.
"We have laid the basis for the revival of our country after years of decline. We have taken difficult and courageous decisions. We have begun to adapt France to its times," he said.

He proposed what he called a new contract for the year 2000 based on four major objectives: "Building a modern state, freeing business and the spirit of enterprise to create the jobs we need, renovating the French social and cultural model, making the big Europe a success at last."

While giving few specific policy details, Juppe pledged to cut public spending, ease the tax burden, continue with privatisation and reduce bureaucratic regulation of companies to stimulate individual enterprise.
But he ruled out more radical "Thatcherite" policies, saying the coalition would not adopt "simplistic hyperliberalism" but uphold France's social protection system and public services.

Juppe began his keynote address to an invited audience of outgoing Gaullist and centre-right UDF parliamentarians 20 minutes late in a Paris congress centre beneath the giant slogan "With Jacques Chirac, a new impulse for France."
